overview: The atlas paints “Eeyou Istchee” across one approximate 1492 to 1500 polygon and imports a modern Quebec summary, but neither field proves a fifteenth-century state or surveyed frontier. Cree Nation Government says, “We call ourselves Eeyou,” glosses Eeyou Istchee as the People’s Land, and describes a living nation of distinct communities and family hunting territories. Those present institutions and land categories must not be projected backward. This card instead pairs the map layer with bounded regional archaeology, community knowledge, and carefully dated later evidence about seasonal work, families, teaching, language, health, water, and governance. The decoded polygon overlaps nine other atlas labels, shares arcs with Inuit, Nunavik, and Moose Cree layers, excludes present-day Waskaganish, and assigns several places to multiple owners. It is therefore an editorial sketch, not a census or title deed. Eight one-year bands organize the atlas interval without inventing annual events. Modern Eastern James Bay Cree sources preserve knowledge and continuity, while every later comparison keeps its date. The 1500 endpoint marks another atlas repaint; Eeyou people, communities, languages, and land relations continue.

periods.title: An approximate atlas layer appears
periods.summary: The 1492 snapshot introduces this exact id for one eight-year interval. No source records a capital, monarch, founding act, surveyed border, or event in 1492. The first band therefore explains the database layer itself, including its approximate dating and incorrect imported state classification, rather than inventing a political beginning.

periods.title: Archaeology reaches beyond the interval
periods.summary: Nothing securely marks 1493 as a special year. A regional land-use study instead summarizes archaeological evidence near Waskaganish reaching back about 4,200 years. That deep record establishes long human presence in the region, while its broad chronology and secondary synthesis cannot name one household or map a precise 1493 boundary.

periods.title: Stone work records movement and skill
periods.summary: No annual event is assigned to 1494. Aanischaaukamikw describes undated pre-contact workshops near Oujé-Bougoumou with thousands of stone artifacts, local raw material, and some Mistassini quartzite. The evidence supports toolmaking and movement, yet poor dating and limited cultural attribution prevent turning the workshop into a named 1494 Eeyou village.

periods.title: Family territories require careful history
periods.summary: The atlas offers no 1495 land register. Colin Scott reviews family hunting territories as flexible systems of authority, access, sharing, and collective validation whose history has been debated. His evidence helps explain later Eeyou stewardship, but a modern trapline map or tallyman system cannot simply be copied onto the fifteenth century.

periods.title: Oral knowledge carried history
periods.summary: No local manuscript securely dates to 1496. Aanischaaukamikw says Cree history is primarily oral and has been passed between generations, with Elders guiding teaching resources and recorded stories. This supports disciplined learning and memory, while offering no verbatim transcript of a tale, lesson, or conversation during this editorial year.

periods.title: Language lived before modern dictionaries
periods.summary: No dictionary was compiled in 1497. The East Cree Language Resource Project now documents Northern and Southern varieties, hundreds of stories, teaching materials, and a dictionary first published in 2004. These living resources can illustrate language accurately today; their modern spellings cannot be presented as a surviving fifteenth-century page.

periods.title: The interval predates trading posts
periods.summary: No source identifies first contact in 1498. The land-use synthesis places trading posts on principal navigation routes only toward the end of the seventeenth century. Its earlier description of scattered hunting groups and summer fishing gatherings is broad regional reconstruction, not an annual diary, and later posts must remain outside this atlas band.

periods.title: The color changes and continuity remains
periods.summary: No collapse, conquest, migration, or collective death ends the interval. In 1500 the exact id disappears and sampled places receive other broad labels; 1530 repaints the region again. Those file changes are atlas seams. They cannot end Eeyou history, erase neighboring peoples, or define the modern Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee.

sections.title: Read the atlas boundary with care

items.text: The imported index dates Eeyou Istchee approximately 1492 to 1500, while coverage calls it a state and the summary describes modern Quebec institutions. These fields document unfinished atlas metadata. They do not establish a fifteenth-century government, capital, tax system, legal boundary, or single authority over everyone inside the color.

Decoded from the 1492 topology, the feature is one Polygon with one closed ring, 105 stored positions, and 104 unique positions. Its bounding box runs about 79.67° to 69.32° west and 48.20° to 56.68° north. Geometry describes the file precisely, not historical jurisdiction.

Exact ring tests find area overlap with nine atlas labels, including Cree, Inuit, Moose Cree, Innu, Naskapi, Algonquin, Atikamekw, Abitibiwinni, and Nunavik layers. Shared arcs connect the target directly to Inuit, Nunavik, and Moose Cree shapes. The map therefore encodes overlapping editorial categories, not exclusive borders.

Cree Nation Government describes Eeyouch today in eastern James Bay and southeastern Hudson Bay, while present institutions bring together executive and administrative branches. That living political geography cannot be reduced to one 1492 file color, which neither decides community boundaries nor locates every Eeyou family.

The exact id appears in the 1492 snapshot but not in the checked 1400, 1500, or 1530 snapshots. Broad “Subarctic Forest Hunter-Gatherers” labels cover much of the region in nearby files, while some points switch to Thule or Algonquin categories. The sequence records cartographic repainting, not an eight-year Eeyou rise and fall.

sections.title: Let archaeology show presence without false precision

items.text: A land-use study summarizes the earliest recorded occupation near Waskaganish at about 4,200 years ago, on the Broadback River. That date shows deep regional history, not an unbroken ownership certificate. It cannot identify every ancient visitor as Eeyou or assign a specific camp to the atlas years 1492 to 1500.

Aanischaaukamikw reports pre-contact workshops near Oujé-Bougoumou where stone tools were made, including knives, scrapers, points, hammerstones, and abundant flakes. Reliable charcoal and burned bone were absent, so investigators could not assign precise dates. “Pre-contact” is a useful ceiling, not a secret code for 1494.

Excavation at one Oujé-Bougoumou-area site recovered 5,865 artifacts from 30 square metres, mostly local stone suited to chipping. Some Mistassini quartzite suggests travelers or contacts. The institute explicitly says evidence for cultural identity remains meagre, so material movement must not become an automatic ethnic label.

A regional synthesis defines late paleohistory broadly as about 2,000 to 400 BP. It reports southern summer gatherings, elongated multi-family dwellings, waterside sites, varied fauna, stone, pottery, and ochre, alongside northern caribou patterns. The interval includes 1492, but these differences resist one homogeneous atlas-year portrait.

Aanischaaukamikw’s main collection brings historical Eeyou objects together from many institutions and invites community members to add knowledge. Museum catalogues can reconnect makers, materials, places, and stories. Their current categories are research tools, however, not a complete inventory of what every family owned in 1492.

sections.title: Follow seasons, food, and respectful harvesting

items.text: A modern environment-and-health study asks how often people hunt, fish, and eat traditional foods, and how those activities relate to nutrition, contaminants, animals, and water. It confirms that land foods remain important. Contemporary survey answers cannot reconstruct one fifteenth-century menu, season, or family’s share.

Aanischaaukamikw’s autumn fish-smoking demonstration linked spawning trout, cleaning fish, building a smoke dome, and preserving food for winter. Visitors and community members joined the work. This dated teaching event illustrates continuing skill and social learning, while never pretending that its parking-lot setup is a photographed 1492 camp.

A Cree-Innu caribou understanding uses elder guidance, sharing, sustainable harvest, respect for animals, local authorization, and tallymen. It responds to a modern population decline and relations between living nations. Those explicit circumstances matter: the agreement cannot be quoted as a timeless hunting code for every fifteenth-century group.

Cree Health connects present Eeyou family values with land, birds, fish, animals harvested for food, respect, and gratitude. The page offers community philosophy rather than an archaeological report. It supports living continuity and relational ethics, but cannot specify how much meat, fish, or berries a 1492 household ate.

An ethnobotanical survey interviewed 34 Cree Elders and recorded 18 plants associated with 15 diabetes-related symptoms. It demonstrates detailed plant knowledge and community research collaboration. Because the project addresses a modern disease concern and is explicitly non-exhaustive, its species list is not a fifteenth-century pantry or pharmacy catalogue.

sections.title: Make clothing, tools, boats, and preserved food

items.text: Aanischaaukamikw’s “Footprints” exhibition assembled about 150 objects, including snowshoes, moccasins, parkas, mittens, and hunting and trapping tools. Materials and techniques display Eeyou skill and artistry. Museum pieces from different dates cannot be bundled into one 1492 kit, yet they make technological variety plainly visible.

Aanischaaukamikw’s “Footprints” exhibition included children’s ceremonial outfits beside snowshoes, clothing, and hunting and trapping tools. The display makes scale, materials, and skilled making visible across generations. Because the objects have different histories, their grouping cannot establish one complete child’s outfit or tool kit for 1492.

The current Eastern James Bay Cree dictionary writes ᒌᒫᓐ as chiimaan and glosses it as “boat” or “ship”; the Waswanipi entry also includes canoe. A secure word shows living language and transport vocabulary. It does not date a vessel, specify its construction, or make modern spelling a 1492 inscription.

Aanischaaukamikw traced a rabbit-fur coat through one Wemindji family, prompting memories of camp food, a maker, mittens, and a hat. The object became a meeting place for stories. That family-specific biography is stronger than generic “Cree clothing” and still remains much later than the atlas interval.

Smoking fish required catching and cleaning it, building a dome, tending a small fire, and judging when preservation was complete. Aanischaaukamikw’s demonstration drew many helpers and tasters. The gentle archaeological lesson is that smoke may announce supper, but it does not identify a fifteenth-century cook from miles away.

sections.title: Meet families, children, and shared responsibilities

items.text: Colin Scott describes family territories as systems nested within wider community relationships, not fenced private parcels. Historical accounts and modern Eeyou law allow travel, fishing, and berry gathering under conditions of respect and sharing. The history remains debated, so today’s registered traplines cannot simply be projected onto 1492.

Scott’s review notes that travelers crossing another family territory could fish when food was needed and were expected to share with hosts they met. Modern written hunting law also stresses informing territory leaders and preventing waste. These sources reveal responsibilities and flexibility, not a timeless cadastral code.

At Aanischaaukamikw’s Family Weekend, children and parents learned syllabics, mothers and daughters sewed and beaded, and a Chisasibi healer spoke about children’s rites of passage. The event makes intergenerational learning concrete. Its program is modern and cannot document an identical gathering five centuries earlier.

Cree Health’s family-values page links children, parents, grandparents, community, land, respect, and gratitude. It presents care as a shared living responsibility rather than an isolated household task. The page documents contemporary Eeyou teaching and philosophy; it cannot supply the exact membership or duties of a family camp in 1492.

A Cree Nation declaration affirms children’s rights to education and traditional knowledge, health and social services, participation in decisions, clean drinking water, protected lands and traditional foods, and accountable governments. It is a contemporary rights statement by living institutions, not the words of an undocumented fifteenth-century council.

sections.title: Learn from land, stories, Elders, and schools

items.text: The Cree School Board says youth traditionally learned from families while living on the land, practicing hunting, trapping, sewing, cooking, and other skills. This institutional history describes a broad educational pattern. It cannot tell us the lesson order, age, teacher, or exact activity of one child in 1492.

Aanischaaukamikw says Cree history is primarily oral, passed between generations, and that Elders guide its teaching content. Recorded stories and legends now support classrooms and visitors. Oral learning is not an evidence gap disguised as folklore; it is knowledge transmission, although no webpage recovers a verbatim 1496 performance.

The East Cree project lists dated conversation manuals, dialect resource books, a 2009 syllabics workbook, mathematics terminology, stories, dictionaries, and literacy tools. Modern educators combine sound, print, grammar, and community authorship. These resources demonstrate active language teaching, not a school curriculum frozen unchanged since the fifteenth century.

The Cree School Board’s 2019 to 2020 report lists Cree History and Citizenship, language development, land-based programs, teacher training, literacy certification, and elder video interviews. These are specific modern educational achievements. Their institutional form should be celebrated without being backdated into a fifteenth-century classroom or ministry.

Cree Nation Government supports place names, archaeology, traditional knowledge, language planning, public education, youth, women, and Elders. That network shows learning across institutions and generations today. It also separates current governance from the atlas layer: a modern department is not evidence of a bureaucracy operating inside the 1492 polygon.

sections.title: Hear language varieties and read one modern word

items.text: Eastern James Bay Cree has Northern and Southern dialects with different spelling conventions. Wemindji, Chisasibi, and Whapmagoostui are listed with Northern; most inland communities and Waskaganish with Southern; Eastmain chose Southern spelling in a transitional area. One sample therefore cannot represent every Eeyou voice.

Written sample: ᓂᐲ. The modern dictionary gives the roman form “nipii” and the English meaning “water,” marking it as an inanimate noun in Northern East Cree. This exact, secure teaching sample belongs to the current dictionary. It is not a surviving page, carving, or standardized spelling from 1492.

No source in this packet supplies a securely dated Eeyou manuscript from 1492 to 1500. The online language project began in 2000, and its English-Cree dictionary first appeared in 2004. Showing modern syllabics openly fills a learning need without fabricating a fifteenth-century written document or claiming speech began with writing.

The Northern spelling guide says community, age, pronunciation, and learning history produce variation, while recent dictionaries incorporate agreed revisions. Small final symbols and other conventions map sounds systematically. Orthographic standardization helps readers across communities, but it should not erase distinct speaking styles or be pushed backward five centuries.

The Interactive East Cree Reference Grammar separates Northern and Southern grammars and links sound, spelling, syllabic charts, and verb forms. Marie-Odile Junker dates the edited resource 2000 to 2019. Its digital precision is a modern achievement built with speakers and teachers, not evidence of medieval computer-ready orthography.

sections.title: Discuss health and caregiving without prescribing

items.text: Researchers interviewed 34 Cree Elders about plants associated with diabetes symptoms, then ranked 18 species for further study. That careful method records knowledge and uncertainty. It is not a prescription, an exhaustive pharmacopoeia, or proof that each plant was used identically in every community during the atlas interval.

Cree Health’s medicine-card project credits traditional knowledge keepers and names balsam fir, cedar, sage, sweetgrass, tamarack, tobacco, and white spruce. It directs readers toward knowledgeable people rather than self-treatment. The project documents living practice and revitalization; it does not date every use to 1492.

A current Cree midwifery program combines competencies equivalent to university programs with cultural and traditional knowledge, remote-birth emergency skills, and community health education. This is a major modern care achievement. It should not be used to invent a fifteenth-century clinic, license, birth protocol, or universal household practice.

The environment-and-health study connects nutrition, contaminants, hunting, fishing, wildlife, drinking water, and illness. Its design shows that health is relational and place-specific. Because research ran in 2005 to 2009, its questionnaires and laboratory results cannot diagnose people five centuries earlier or reveal undocumented epidemic history.

Cree Health presents Iiyiyiuiyihtuwin, the Eeyou/Eenou way of life, and family values through land, food, gratitude, relationships, and responsibility. That community framework widens “health” beyond a list of remedies. It remains a living, current articulation; readers should not convert it into one timeless medical doctrine.

sections.title: Handle water, wastewater, toilets, and evidence gaps

items.text: The reviewed evidence does not identify a fifteenth-century Eeyou toilet, latrine, sewer, refuse schedule, or universal washing rule. A Cree Health report begins its documented infrastructure history much later. This bounded gap avoids two bad guesses: imagining modern plumbing in 1492 or assuming families had no sanitation practices at all.

Cree Health reports that rivers, lakes, springs, wells, and melted snow supplied drinking and washing water, while community water and sewage systems brought running water and flush toilets into homes only in the 1980s. The dated decade cleanly prevents modern fixtures from being back-projected into the atlas interval.

Current bush-water guidance advises checking sources, boiling when needed, using suitable containers, protecting family members from burns, and choosing one place for wastewater. These practical instructions address present health conditions. They document modern care around water and waste, not a word-for-word fifteenth-century camp rule.

Cree Health reports that some spring and stream water stored in containers contained enough germs to cause illness, and warns against plastic garbage bags for storage. The advice is deliberately current and medical. It should inform present safety, not be recast as proof of ancient germ theory.

Cree Nation Government’s Capital Works department supports essential sanitation, housing inspection, drinking-water treatment, and wastewater services in communities. Those systems are contemporary public infrastructure. Their existence demonstrates living governance and engineering while confirming that the atlas polygon cannot stand in for today’s service area or legal authority.

The Grand Council and Cree Nation Government now represent the coming together of the executive and administrative branches of Cree government. This structure is a modern political achievement by living Eeyouch. It must be described on its own dates, not used to validate the imported claim of a 1492 state.

The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement was signed on 11 November 1975 after Cree and Inuit legal action over hydroelectric development. Later agreements expanded governance, forestry, marine, and constitutional arrangements. These negotiated institutions demonstrate political strength and adaptation; they are not continuations of an atlas border unchanged since 1492.

The Cree School Board was officially constituted on 28 June 1978 after the JBNQA, returning major educational authority to Eeyou institutions. Its story also records the harm of imposed schooling. Building schools, teacher programs, language resources, and land-based curricula is continuity through self-determination, not a return to an imagined frozen past.

Aanischaaukamikw is a Cree-led museum and cultural institute whose collections, databases, and acquisitions reconnect objects with community knowledge. It welcomes additions from community members and supports research access. Cultural stewardship here is active work: preserving an object also means preserving questions, names, memories, and authority over interpretation.

The Eeyou Marine Region agreement recognizes Cree harvesting, planning, wildlife, impact-review, and archaeological roles while also recording joint Cree-Inuit ownership in part of the region. That modern legal complexity is an achievement and a warning: even today, territorial relationships overlap, so the atlas’s single colored line cannot be timeless.

ending.text: The atlas removes the exact Eeyou Istchee id in 1500 and repaints much of the area with broad categories. It records no battle, surrender, evacuation, epidemic, or political dissolution in that year. Later events belong on later dates. Cree Nation Government’s timeline begins its detailed modern milestones with the 1971 hydroelectric announcement, when Eeyou communities were not consulted and hunting territories faced flooding. It records the 1973 court victory, creation of the Grand Council in 1974, the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, later governance and marine agreements, Cree language legislation, and the 2021 election of the first woman Grand Chief. These achievements followed profound colonial pressure and environmental change; they do not prove that the imported polygon was an ancient state. Nor does modern government replace the histories of individual First Nations, families, neighboring Inuit, Innu, Naskapi, Algonquin, Atikamekw, Moose Cree, or other Cree peoples. The responsible ending is continuity across a software seam. The layer stops in 1500. Eeyou/Eenou people, communities, language varieties, land relationships, knowledge, and political life continue.
